title: I Asked My Husband to Watch Our Four Kids for 20 Minutes While I Showered, and What the Camera Showed Me Changed Everything
fb_text:
I asked my husband to watch our four young children for just twenty minutes while I took a shower. When I came back, he was furious and said they had ruined his evening. I apologized, feeling guilty, until I checked our living room security camera and saw something I never expected.

My husband and I have four children under five, and one twenty-minute shower made me question everything I thought I understood about our marriage.

We have a four-year-old daughter, three-year-old twin girls, and a one-year-old son.

I'm a stay-at-home mom, and almost every part of our children's daily routine falls on me, from the moment they wake up until they go to bed. My husband works in an office, and over time we settled into a routine that I was too exhausted to question.

In his eyes, bringing home a paycheck means he's done his part. Once he walks through the door, he considers his day over. He expects dinner on the table, a tidy house, and a peaceful evening with no interruptions.

My duties, on the other hand, never really end. I love our children dearly, but looking after four little ones practically around the clock has worn me down, body and soul.

By last Tuesday, I was running on empty. I hadn't had a proper shower in over two days, because there was always someone who needed to be fed, changed, comforted, or watched.

Then, around seven that evening, I finally got a small window.

All four children had already had their baths, put on their pajamas, and settled in the living room. Our youngest was happily busy in his playpen, and the three girls sat quietly watching cartoons.

For once that day, nobody needed me right away.

My husband was resting in his usual recliner, so I asked if he could keep an eye on the kids for twenty minutes while I showered.

I wasn't asking him to cook, clean, or entertain them. All I wanted was for him to stay close and make sure they were safe and comfortable.

He let out an impatient sigh before agreeing, barely looking up at me.

I hurried to the bathroom. I can't remember ever showering so fast. There was no time to enjoy the warm water or unwind. I rushed through it, worried one of the children might need something before I was done.

I was back in the living room in less than twenty minutes.

All four children were still exactly where I'd left them.

But my husband had moved to the couch. He sat stiffly, visibly irritated.

I softly asked if something had happened.

He snapped right away. He said I was inconsiderate for expecting him to look after four children when he'd planned to relax after a long day at work.

According to him, it had been incredibly hard. He insisted that for those twenty minutes they had been shouting, fighting over toys, climbing all over him, and refusing to settle down.

He also complained that my little "spa session" had completely destroyed the peaceful evening he'd been looking forward to.

His words left me feeling terribly guilty. Instead of questioning what he said, I apologized over and over. I told him I never meant to make things difficult for him and promised not to ask again.

Then I took the children upstairs, got them into bed, and felt embarrassed that I'd needed twenty minutes just to take care of my own hygiene.

Later that evening, I was alone in the kitchen finishing the dishes. My husband had already gone up to bed, still looking annoyed, while I kept working through what was left of the household chores.

As I washed the plates, I kept replaying his complaints and wondering if my request really had been unreasonable.

Then I remembered that our youngest had lost his pacifier somewhere in the living room.

We had installed a security camera with a wide-angle view of most of that area. It occurred to me that the recording might show where the pacifier had ended up.

I picked up my phone, opened the security camera app, and started watching the footage from those twenty minutes.

article_html:
My husband and I have four children under five, and a single twenty-minute shower made me question everything I thought I understood about our marriage.

We have a four-year-old daughter, three-year-old twin girls, and a one-year-old son. I'm a stay-at-home mom, so almost every part of their daily routine falls on me, from the moment they wake up until bedtime. My husband works in an office, and over time we settled into a pattern I was too tired to question.

In his mind, bringing home a paycheck means he has done his part. When he walks through the door, his day is over. He expects dinner ready, a tidy house, and a peaceful evening. My duties never really end. I love our children dearly, but caring for four little ones around the clock had worn me down physically and emotionally.

The Shower I Almost Couldn't Take

Last Tuesday, I hadn't had a proper shower in over two days. Around seven that evening, I finally saw a small window. All four children had bathed, put on pajamas, and settled in the living room. Our son was happy in his playpen, and the girls were quietly watching cartoons.

My husband was in his recliner, so I asked if he could keep an eye on them for twenty minutes. I wasn't asking him to cook, clean, or entertain anyone. I only wanted him nearby to make sure they were safe. He sighed impatiently and agreed without really looking at me.

I showered faster than I ever have, too worried to enjoy the warm water. I was back in under twenty minutes. All four children were exactly where I'd left them, but my husband was now on the couch, stiff and irritated.

"You Ruined My Evening"

When I asked what was wrong, he snapped. He said I was inconsiderate to expect him to handle four children after a long day. He claimed they had shouted, fought over toys, climbed all over him, and refused to settle down. Then he said my "spa session" had destroyed the peaceful evening he'd been looking forward to.

I felt terribly guilty. I apologized again and again, promised never to ask again, and took the children up to bed, embarrassed that I'd needed twenty minutes for something as basic as washing.

What the Camera Showed

Later, I was alone in the kitchen doing dishes while my husband sulked upstairs. I kept wondering whether my request had really been unreasonable. Then I remembered our son had lost his pacifier somewhere in the living room. Our security camera covers most of that space, so I opened the app to look for it.

I never found the pacifier on that footage. I found something else.

The girls sat on the rug, watching cartoons exactly as I'd left them. No shouting, no fighting, no climbing. My son played in his playpen and babbled to himself. And my husband? He never put down his phone. For nearly the whole twenty minutes, he scrolled with his feet up, never glancing at the children.

Once, my son tossed a toy out of the playpen and fussed for a moment. My husband looked up, turned the TV volume higher, and went back to his phone. Only near the end did he get up and move to the couch, a few minutes before I walked in.

I watched it twice. The "chaos" he'd described had never happened. The children had been good. He had simply been annoyed that anyone had asked something of him, and I had spent the evening apologizing for it.

The Conversation

I didn't wake him. I sat at the kitchen table for a long while, and what I felt wasn't rage but clarity. I had been so exhausted that I'd accepted his version of events without a second thought.

The next morning, once the kids were fed, I asked him calmly to sit down. I played the footage for him without a word. He watched in silence, his face slowly changing.

At first he tried to explain. He said he was tired, that he hadn't meant it the way it sounded. I told him I wasn't angry about the phone. I was hurt that he'd made me feel like a bad mother and an inconsiderate wife for asking for twenty minutes. I told him that being home with four children isn't a vacation, and that I needed a partner, not a boss who clocks out at the front door.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said he was sorry, and for the first time in a long while, it sounded real. He admitted he had never truly looked at how much I carried, because I never complained loudly enough for him to notice.

A Small but Real Change

We didn't fix everything in one conversation. But he agreed to take over bath time and bedtime three nights a week, and to watch the children so I can shower, or simply sit alone in a quiet room, without a sigh or a speech afterward.

Last Friday, he did bath time on his own. I heard splashing, laughing, and one very loud twin. When he came downstairs, soaked and a little frazzled, he said quietly, "I don't know how you do this every day."

I smiled. For once, I didn't apologize.
